pois.name: Bismarck: main hull
pois.note: Uses the 2001 expedition’s published vicinity (48.15 N, 16.117 W), not a precise survey fix. Terrain reads 4,218.5 m; the scan at 4,213 m is about 5 m above it. Published real wreck depth is 4,790–4,791 m. The ~570 m coordinate/grid/depth discrepancy is unresolved; no sourced cause or more precise fix was established. The hull remains supported on the current terrain. See sources.md.

pois.name: Detached main gun turrets
pois.note: The four main turrets fell out during capsizing. This authored marker and matching prop sit about 600 m east-northeast and upslope of the hull (moved 2026-11 from about 900 m so the dive is a short route; the 2001 expedition identified one turret near the hull). Public individual turret coordinates are not available; the layout follows the general slope setting rather than surveyed turret positions.

pois.name: Battle damage: shell and torpedo hits
pois.note: Marks the historical question, not a single surveyed feature: whether British shellfire and torpedoes, or the crew's own scuttling charges, caused the final sinking. kbismarck.com's survey notes describe the hull as in surprisingly good condition given the battering it took, with the stern the most heavily damaged section. Illustrative placement near the hull; moved 2026-09 with the hull to the sourced wreck position (see sources.md).

pois.name: Memorial marker
pois.note: Restored 2026-11. A respectful marker near the hull, not a surveyed structure or a prop. Of Bismarck's crew of 2,221, only around 114 were rescued; roughly 2,100 died. This game has no salvage, collection or loot of any kind at any site.

pois.name: The seamount flank
pois.note: Real survey data. Restored 2026-11 about 300 m up-slope (north-east) of the hull so the dive's route reaches it: this tile's terrain shoals from 4,218.5 m at the hull to about 4,207 m here, and on to about 4,182 m some 500 m up-slope, toward the seamount summit (~4,024 m about 3 km further along the same line). Published accounts describe the real debris trail as about 1 km long down a much steeper (~14.5 degree) slope, formed when the turrets hit the seamount first and triggered a landslide that carried the hull further down -- so this point sits between the turret-debris marker (further up-slope) and the hull (down-slope), on the same real slope. This tile's grid, built from GMRT's coarser global (GEBCO-derived) fill rather than a dedicated survey of the wreck site, is far too coarse to resolve the true trail or slope angle -- what you scan here is real but smoothed terrain, not the skid mark itself.
